The colour of the wheels in Ezekiel’s vision was as the colour of a beryl stone (1:16; 10:9; R.V., “stone of Tarshish”). It is mentioned in ⟦22.5.14|아 5:14⟧; ⟦27.10.6|단 10:6⟧; ⟦66.21.20|계 21:20⟧. In ⟦26.28.13|겔 28:13⟧ the LXX. render the word by “chrysolite,” which the Jewish historian Josephus regards as its proper translation. This also is the rendering given in the Authorized Version in the margin. That was a gold-coloured gem, the topaz of ancient authors.
The rendering of a Hebrew word meaning sweeper, occurs only in ⟦23.14.23|사 14:23⟧, of the sweeping away, the utter ruin, of Babylon.

Cold, a ravine or brook in the extreme south-west of Judah, where 200 of David’s men stayed behind because they were faint, while the other 400 pursued the Amalekites (⟦9.30.9|삼상 30:9⟧, ⟦9.30.10|10⟧, ⟦9.30.21|21⟧). Probably the Wadyes Sheriah, south of Gaza.
The rendering in ⟦23.8.21|사 8:21⟧, where alone it occurs, of a Hebrew word meaning to oppress, or be in circumstances of hardship.
Confidence, a city belonging to Hadadezer, king of Zobah, which yielded much spoil of brass to David (⟦10.8.8|삼하 8:8⟧). In ⟦13.18.8|대상 18:8⟧ it is called Tibhath.
Occurs frequently as the appellation for a house, or dwelling-place, in such compounds as the words immediately following:

House of the ford, a place on the east bank of the Jordan, where John was baptizing (⟦43.1.28|요 1:28⟧). It may be identical with Bethbarah, the ancient ford of Jordan of which the men of Ephraim took possession (⟦7.7.24|삿 7:24⟧). The Revised Version reads “Bethany beyond Jordan.” It was the great ford, and still bears the name of “the ford,” Makhadhet ‘Abarah, “the ford of crossing over,” about 25 miles from Nazareth.
House of response, one of the fenced cities of Naphtali (⟦6.19.38|수 19:38⟧). It is perhaps identical with the modern village ‘Ainata, 6 miles west of Kedesh.
House of answers, a city in the mountainous district of Judah (⟦6.15.59|수 15:59⟧). It has been identified with the modern Beit-‘Anun, about 3 miles northeast of Hebron.

House of dates.
1. The Revised Version in ⟦43.1.28|요 1:28⟧ has this word instead of Bethabara, on the authority of the oldest manuscripts. It appears to have been the name of a place on the east of Jordan.
2. A village on the south-eastern slope of the Mount of Olives (⟦41.11.1|막 11:1⟧), about 2 miles east of Jerusalem, on the road to Jericho. It derived its name from the number of palm-trees which grew there. It was the residence of Lazarus and his sisters. It is frequently mentioned in connection with memorable incidents in the life of our Lord (⟦40.21.17|마 21:17⟧; ⟦40.26.6|26:6⟧; ⟦41.11.11|막 11:11⟧, ⟦41.11.12|12⟧; ⟦41.14.3|14:3⟧; ⟦42.24.50|눅 24:50⟧; ⟦43.11.1|요 11:1⟧; ⟦43.12.1|12:1⟧). It is now known by the name of el-Azariyeh, i.e., “place of Lazarus,” or simply Lazariyeh. Seen from a distance, the village has been described as “remarkably beautiful, the perfection of retirement and repose, of seclusion and lovely peace.” Now a mean village, containing about twenty families.

House of the desert, one of the six cities of Judah, situated in the sunk valley of the Jordan and Dead Sea (⟦6.18.22|수 18:22⟧). In ⟦6.15.61|수 15:61⟧ it is said to have been “in the wilderness.” It was afterwards included in the towns of Benjamin. It is called Arabah (⟦6.18.18|수 18:18⟧).

House of the height; i.e., “mountain-house”, one of the towns of Gad, 3 miles east of Jordan, opposite Jericho (⟦6.13.27|수 13:27⟧). Probably the same as Beth-haran in ⟦4.32.36|민 32:36⟧. It was called by king Herod, Julias, or Livias, after Livia, the wife of Augustus. It is now called Beit-haran.

House of God’s court, a place alluded to by Hosea (10:14) as the scene of some great military exploit, but not otherwise mentioned in Scripture. The Shalman here named was probably Shalmaneser, the king of Assyria (⟦12.17.3|왕하 17:3⟧).

House of nothingness; i.e., “of idols”, a place in the mountains of Benjamin, east of Bethel (⟦6.7.2|수 7:2⟧; ⟦6.18.12|18:12⟧; ⟦9.13.5|삼상 13:5⟧). In ⟦28.4.15|호 4:15⟧; ⟦28.5.8|5:8⟧; ⟦28.10.5|10:5⟧ it stands for “Bethel” (q.v.), and it is so called because it was no longer the “house of God,” but “the house of idols,” referring to the calves there worshipped.

House of crossing, a place south of the scene of Gideon’s victory (⟦7.7.24|삿 7:24⟧). It was probably the chief ford of the Jordan in that district, and may have been that by which Jacob crossed when he returned from Mesopotamia, near the Jabbok (⟦1.32.22|창 32:22⟧), and at which Jephthah slew the Ephraimites (⟦7.12.4|삿 12:4⟧). Nothing, however, is certainly known of it.
Sheep-house, a place to which the Israelites pursued the Philistines west from Mizpeh (⟦9.7.11|삼상 7:11⟧).

House of Dagon.
1. A city in the low country or plain of Judah, near Philistia (⟦6.15.41|수 15:41⟧); the modern Beit Degan, about 5 miles from Lydda.
2. A city near the south-east border of Asher (⟦6.19.27|수 19:27⟧). It was a Philistine colony. It is identical with the modern ruined village of Tell D’auk.
House of two cakes of figs, a city of Moab, upon which Jeremiah (48:22) denounced destruction. It is called also Almon-diblathaim (⟦4.33.46|민 33:46⟧) and Diblath (⟦26.6.14|겔 6:14⟧). (R.V., “Diblah.”)

House of God.
1. A place in Central Palestine, about 10 miles north of Jerusalem, at the head of the pass of Michmash and Ai. It was originally the royal Canaanite city of Luz (⟦1.28.19|창 28:19⟧). The name Bethel was at first apparently given to the sanctuary in the neighbourhood of Luz, and was not given to the city itself till after its conquest by the tribe of Ephraim. When Abram entered Canaan he formed his second encampment between Bethel and Hai (⟦1.12.8|창 12:8⟧); and on his return from Egypt he came back to it, and again “called upon the name of the Lord” (13:4). Here Jacob, on his way from Beersheba to Haran, had a vision of the angels of God ascending and descending on the ladder whose top reached unto heaven (28:10, 19); and on his return he again visited this place, “where God talked with him” (35:1-15), and there he “built an altar, and called the place El-beth-el” (q.v.). To this second occasion of God’s speaking with Jacob at Bethel, Hosea (12:4, 5) makes reference.
 In troublous times the people went to Bethel to ask counsel of God (⟦7.20.18|삿 20:18⟧, ⟦7.20.31|31⟧; 21:2). Here the ark of the covenant was kept for a long time under the care of Phinehas, the grandson of Aaron (20:26-28). Here also Samuel held in rotation his court of justice (⟦9.7.16|삼상 7:16⟧). It was included in Israel after the kingdom was divided, and it became one of the seats of the worship of the golden calf (⟦11.12.28|왕상 12:28⟧; ⟦11.13.1|13:1⟧). Hence the prophet Hosea (⟦28.4.15|호 4:15⟧; ⟦28.5.8|5:8⟧; ⟦28.10.5|10:5⟧, ⟦28.10.8|8⟧) calls it in contempt Beth-aven, i.e., “house of idols.” Bethel remained an abode of priests even after the kingdom of Israel was desolated by the king of Assyria (⟦12.17.28|왕하 17:28⟧, ⟦12.17.29|29⟧). At length all traces of the idolatries were extirpated by Josiah, king of Judah (⟦12.23.15|왕하 23:15⟧); and the place was still in existence after the Captivity (⟦15.2.28|스 2:28⟧; ⟦16.7.32|느 7:32⟧). It has been identified with the ruins of Beitin, a small village amid extensive ruins some 9 miles south of Shiloh.
2. Mount Bethel was a hilly district near Bethel (⟦6.16.1|수 16:1⟧; ⟦9.13.2|삼상 13:2⟧).
3. A town in the south of Judah (⟦6.8.17|수 8:17⟧; ⟦6.12.16|12:16⟧).
A designation of Hiel (q.v.), who rebuilt Jericho and experienced the curse pronounced long before (⟦11.16.34|왕상 16:34⟧).
Dissection or separation, certain mountains mentioned in ⟦22.2.17|아 2:17⟧; probably near Lebanon.

House of mercy, a reservoir (Gr. kolumbethra, “a swimming bath”) with five porches, close to the sheep-gate or market (⟦16.3.1|느 3:1⟧; ⟦43.5.2|요 5:2⟧). Eusebius the historian (A.D. 330) calls it “the sheep-pool.” It is also called “Bethsaida” and “Beth-zatha” (⟦43.5.2|요 5:2⟧, R.V. marg.). Under these “porches” or colonnades were usually a large number of infirm people waiting for the “troubling of the water.” It is usually identified with the modern so-called Fountain of the Virgin, in the valley of the Kidron, and not far from the Pool of Siloam (q.v.); and also with the Birket Israel, a pool near the mouth of the valley which runs into the Kidron south of “St. Stephen’s Gate.” Others again identify it with the twin pools called the “Souterrains,” under the convent of the Sisters of Zion, situated in what must have been the rock-hewn ditch between Bezetha and the fortress of Antonia. But quite recently Schick has discovered a large tank, as sketched here, situated about 100 feet north-west of St. Anne’s Church, which is, as he contends, very probably the Pool of Bethesda. No certainty as to its identification, however, has as yet been arrived at.
Camel-house, a city in the “plain country” of Moab denounced by the prophet (⟦24.48.23|렘 48:23⟧); probably the modern Um-el-Jemal, near Bozrah, one of the deserted cities of the Hauran.
House of Gilgal, a place from which the inhabitants gathered for the purpose of celebrating the rebuilding of the walls on the return exile (⟦16.12.29|느 12:29⟧).

House of a vineyard, a place in the tribe of Judah (⟦16.3.14|느 3:14⟧) where the Benjamites were to set up a beacon when they heard the trumpet against the invading army of the Babylonians (⟦24.6.1|렘 6:1⟧). It is probable that this place is the modern ‘Ain Karim, or “well of the vineyards,” near which there is a ridge on which are cairns which may have served as beacons of old, one of which is 40 feet high and 130 in diameter.

House of the hollow, or of the cavern, the name of two towns or villages (⟦14.8.5|대하 8:5⟧; ⟦13.7.24|대상 7:24⟧) in the territory of Ephraim, on the way from Jerusalem to Joppa. They are distinguished as Beth-horon “the upper” and Beth-horon “the nether.” They are about 2 miles apart, the former being about 10 miles north-west of Jerusalem. Between the two places was the ascent and descent of Beth-horon, leading from Gibeon down to the western plain (⟦6.10.10|수 10:10⟧, ⟦6.10.11|11⟧; 18:13, 14), down which the five kings of the Amorites were driven by Joshua in that great battle, the most important in which the Hebrews had been as yet engaged, being their first conflict with their enemies in the open field. Jehovah interposed in behalf of Israel by a terrific hailstorm, which caused more deaths among the Canaanites than did the swords of the Israelites. Beth-horon is mentioned as having been taken by Shishak, B.C. 945, in the list of his conquests, and the pass was the scene of a victory of Judas Maccabeus. (Comp. ⟦2.9.19|출 9:19⟧, ⟦2.9.25|25⟧; ⟦18.38.22|욥 38:22⟧, ⟦18.38.23|23⟧; ⟦19.18.12|시 18:12⟧; ⟦23.30.30|사 30:30⟧.) The modern name of these places is Beit-ur, distinguished by el-Foka, “the upper,” and el-Tahta, “the nether.” The lower was at the foot of the pass, and the upper, 500 feet higher, at the top, west of Gibeon.

House of wastes, or deserts, a town near Abel-shittim, east of Jordan, in the desert of Moab, where the Israelites encamped not long before crossing the Jordan (⟦4.33.49|민 33:49⟧; A.V., “Bethjesimoth”). It was within the territory of Sihon, king of the Amorites (⟦6.12.3|수 12:3⟧).
(R.V. ⟦33.1.10|미 1:10⟧), house of dust. The Authorized Version reads “in the house of Aphrah.” This is probably the name of a town in the Shephelah, or “low country,” between Joppa and Gaza.

House of bread.
1. A city in the “hill country” of Judah. It was originally called Ephrath (⟦1.35.16|창 35:16⟧, ⟦1.35.19|19⟧; 48:7; ⟦8.4.11|룻 4:11⟧). It was also called Beth-lehem Ephratah (⟦33.5.2|미 5:2⟧), Beth-lehem-judah (⟦9.17.12|삼상 17:12⟧), and “the city of David” (⟦42.2.4|눅 2:4⟧). It is first noticed in Scripture as the place where Rachel died and was buried “by the wayside,” directly to the north of the city (⟦1.48.7|창 48:7⟧). The valley to the east was the scene of the story of Ruth the Moabitess. There are the fields in which she gleaned, and the path by which she and Naomi returned to the town. Here was David’s birth-place, and here also, in after years, he was anointed as king by Samuel (⟦9.16.4|삼상 16:4⟧); and it was from the well of Bethlehem that three of his heroes brought water for him at the risk of their lives when he was in the cave of Adullam (⟦10.23.13|삼하 23:13⟧). But it was distinguished above every other city as the birth-place of “Him whose goings forth have been of old” (⟦40.2.6|마 2:6⟧; comp. ⟦33.5.2|미 5:2⟧). Afterwards Herod, “when he saw that he was mocked of the wise men,” sent and slew “all the children that were in Bethlehem, and in all the coasts thereof, from two years old and under” (⟦40.2.16|마 2:16⟧, ⟦40.2.18|18⟧; ⟦24.31.15|렘 31:15⟧).
 Bethlehem bears the modern name of Beit-Lahm, i.e., “house of flesh.” It is about 5 miles south of Jerusalem, standing at an elevation of about 2,550 feet above the sea, thus 100 feet higher than Jerusalem.
 There is a church still existing, built by Constantine the Great (A.D. 330), called the “Church of the Nativity,” over a grotto or cave called the “holy crypt,” and said to be the “stable” in which Jesus was born. This is perhaps the oldest existing Christian church in the world. Close to it is another grotto, where Jerome the Latin father is said to have spent thirty years of his life in translating the Scriptures into Latin.
2. A city of Zebulun, mentioned only in ⟦6.19.15|수 19:15⟧. Now Beit-Lahm, a ruined village about 6 miles west-north-west of Nazareth.

House of Peor; i.e., “temple of Baal-peor”, a place in Moab, on the east of Jordan, opposite Jericho. It was in the tribe of Reuben (⟦6.13.20|수 13:20⟧; ⟦5.3.29|신 3:29⟧; ⟦5.4.46|4:46⟧). In the “ravine” or valley over against Beth-peor Moses was probably buried (⟦5.34.6|신 34:6⟧).

House of the unripe fig, a village on the Mount of Olives, on the road from Jerusalem to Jericho (⟦40.21.1|마 21:1⟧; ⟦41.11.1|막 11:1⟧; ⟦42.19.29|눅 19:29⟧), and very close to Bethany. It was the limit of a Sabbath-day’s journey from Jerusalem, i.e., 2,000 cubits. It has been identified with the modern Kefr-et-Tur.

House of fish.
1. A town in Galilee, on the west side of the sea of Tiberias, in the “land of Gennesaret.” It was the native place of Peter, Andrew, and Philip, and was frequently resorted to by Jesus (⟦41.6.45|막 6:45⟧; ⟦43.1.44|요 1:44⟧; ⟦43.12.21|12:21⟧). It is supposed to have been at the modern ‘Ain Tabighah, a bay to the north of Gennesaret.
2. A city near which Christ fed 5,000 (⟦42.9.10|눅 9:10⟧; comp. ⟦43.6.17|요 6:17⟧; ⟦40.14.15|마 14:15⟧), and where the blind man had his sight restored (⟦41.8.22|막 8:22⟧), on the east side of the lake, two miles up the Jordan. It stood within the region of Gaulonitis, and was enlarged by Philip the tetrarch, who called it “Julias,” after the emperor’s daughter. Or, as some have supposed, there may have been but one Bethsaida built on both sides of the lake, near where the Jordan enters it. Now the ruins et-Tel.

House of security or rest, a city which belonged to Manasseh (⟦13.7.29|대상 7:29⟧), on the west of Jordan. The bodies of Saul and his sons were fastened to its walls. In Solomon’s time it gave its name to a district (⟦11.4.12|왕상 4:12⟧). The name is found in an abridged form, Bethshan, in ⟦9.31.10|삼상 31:10⟧, ⟦9.31.12|12⟧ and ⟦10.21.12|삼하 21:12⟧. It is on the road from Jerusalem to Damascus, about 5 miles from the Jordan, and 14 from the south end of the Lake of Gennesaret. After the Captivity it was called Scythopolis, i.e., “the city of the Scythians,” who about B.C. 640 came down from the steppes of Southern Russia and settled in different places in Syria. It is now called Beisan.

House of the sun.
1. A sacerdotal city in the tribe of Dan (⟦6.21.16|수 21:16⟧; ⟦9.6.15|삼상 6:15⟧), on the north border of Judah (⟦6.15.10|수 15:10⟧). It was the scene of an encounter between Jehoash, king of Israel, and Amaziah, king of Judah, in which the latter was made prisoner (⟦12.14.11|왕하 14:11⟧, ⟦12.14.13|13⟧). It was afterwards taken by the Philistines (⟦14.28.18|대하 28:18⟧). It is the modern ruined Arabic village ‘Ain-shems, on the north-west slopes of the mountains of Judah, 14 miles west of Jerusalem.
2. A city between Dothan and the Jordan, near the southern border of Issachar (⟦6.19.22|수 19:22⟧), 7 1/2 miles south of Beth-shean. It is the modern Ain-esh-Shemsiyeh.
3. One of the fenced cities of Naphtali (⟦6.19.38|수 19:38⟧), between Mount Tabor and the Jordan. Now Khurbet Shema, 3 miles west of Safed. But perhaps the same as No. 2.
4. An idol sanctuary in Egypt (⟦24.43.13|렘 43:13⟧); called by the Greeks Heliopolis, and by the Egyptians On (q.v.), ⟦1.41.45|창 41:45⟧.
House of apples, a town of Judah, now Tuffuh, 5 miles west of Hebron (⟦6.15.53|수 15:53⟧).

Man of God, or virgin of God, or house of God.
1. The son of Nahor by Milcah; nephew of Abraham, and father of Rebekah (⟦1.22.22|창 22:22⟧, ⟦1.22.23|23⟧; ⟦1.24.15|24:15⟧, ⟦1.24.24|24⟧, ⟦1.24.47|47⟧). He appears in person only once (24:50).
2. A southern city of Judah (⟦13.4.30|대상 4:30⟧); called also Bethul (⟦6.19.4|수 19:4⟧) and Bethel (12:16; ⟦9.30.27|삼상 30:27⟧).

House of rock, a town in the mountains of Judah (⟦6.15.58|수 15:58⟧), about 4 miles to the north of Hebron. It was built by Rehoboam for the defence of his kingdom (⟦14.11.7|대하 11:7⟧). It stood near the modern ed-Dirweh. Its ruins are still seen on a hill which bears the name of Beit-Sur, and which commands the road from Beer-sheba and Hebron to Jerusalem from the south.

To promise “by one’s truth.” Men and women were betrothed when they were engaged to be married. This usually took place a year or more before marriage. From the time of betrothal the woman was regarded as the lawful wife of the man to whom she was betrothed (⟦5.28.30|신 28:30⟧; ⟦7.14.2|삿 14:2⟧, ⟦7.14.8|8⟧; ⟦40.1.18|마 1:18⟧). The term is figuratively employed of the spiritual connection between God and his people (⟦28.2.19|호 2:19⟧, ⟦28.2.20|20⟧).
Married, is used in ⟦23.62.4|사 62:4⟧ metaphorically as the name of Judea: “Thy land shall be married,” i.e., favoured and blessed of the Lord.
To reveal or disclose; an old English word equivalent to “betray” (⟦20.27.16|잠 27:16⟧; ⟦20.29.24|29:24⟧, R.V., “uttereth;” ⟦23.16.3|사 16:3⟧; ⟦40.26.73|마 26:73⟧).

When used with reference to Jordan, signifies in the writings of Moses the west side of the river, as he wrote on the east bank (⟦1.50.10|창 50:10⟧, ⟦1.50.11|11⟧; ⟦5.1.1|신 1:1⟧, ⟦5.1.5|5⟧; 3:8, 20; 4:46); but in the writings of Joshua, after he had crossed the river, it means the east side (⟦6.5.1|수 5:1⟧; ⟦6.12.7|12:7⟧; ⟦6.22.7|22:7⟧).

In the shadow of God; i.e., “under his protection”, the artificer who executed the work of art in connection with the tabernacle in the wilderness (⟦2.31.2|출 31:2⟧; ⟦2.35.30|35:30⟧). He was engaged principally in works of metal, wood, and stone; while Aholiab, who was associated with him and subordinate to him, had the charge of the textile fabrics (36:1, 2; 38:22). He was of the tribe of Judah, the son of Uri, and grandson of Hur (31:2). Mention is made in ⟦15.10.30|스 10:30⟧ of another of the same name.

Lightning.
1. The residence of Adoni-bezek, in the lot of Judah (⟦7.1.5|삿 1:5⟧). It was in the mountains, not far from Jerusalem. Probably the modern Bezkah, 6 miles south-east of Lydda.
2. The place where Saul numbered the forces of Israel and Judah (⟦9.11.8|삼상 11:8⟧); somewhere in the centre of the country, near the Jordan valley. Probably the modern Ibzik, 13 miles north-east of Shechem.

Ore of gold or silver.
1. A city of the Reubenites; one of the three cities of refuge on the east of Jordan (⟦5.4.1|신 4장⟧: 43; ⟦6.20.8|수 20:8⟧). It has been identified with the modern ruined village of Burazin, some 12 miles north of Heshbon; also with Kasur-el-Besheir, 2 miles south-west of Dibon.
2. A descendant of Asher (⟦13.7.37|대상 7:37⟧).

Bible, the English form of the Greek name Biblia, meaning “books,” the name which in the fifth century began to be given to the entire collection of sacred books, the “Library of Divine Revelation.” The name Bible was adopted by Wickliffe, and came gradually into use in our English language. The Bible consists of sixty-six different books, composed by many different writers, in three different languages, under different circumstances; writers of almost every social rank, statesmen and peasants, kings, herdsmen, fishermen, priests, tax-gatherers, tentmakers; educated and uneducated, Jews and Gentiles; most of them unknown to each other, and writing at various periods during the space of about 1600 years: and yet, after all, it is only one book dealing with only one subject in its numberless aspects and relations, the subject of man’s redemption.
 It is divided into the Old Testament, containing thirty-nine books, and the New Testament, containing twenty-seven books. The names given to the Old in the writings of the New are “the scriptures” (⟦40.21.42|마 21:42⟧), “scripture” (2 Pet. 1:20), “the holy scriptures” (⟦45.1.2|롬 1:2⟧), “the law” (⟦43.12.34|요 12:34⟧), “the law of Moses, the prophets, and the psalms” (⟦42.24.44|눅 24:44⟧), “the law and the prophets” (⟦40.5.17|마 5:17⟧), “the old covenant” (⟦47.3.14|고후 3:14⟧, R.V.). There is a break of 400 years between the Old Testament and the New.
 The Old Testament is divided into three parts:, 1. The Law (Torah), consisting of the Pentateuch, or five books of Moses. 2. The Prophets, consisting of (1) the former, namely, Joshua, Judges, the Books of Samuel, and the Books of Kings; (2) the latter, namely, the greater prophets, Isaiah, Jeremiah, and Ezekiel, and the twelve minor prophets. 3. The Hagiographa, or holy writings, including the rest of the books. These were ranked in three divisions:, (1) The Psalms, Proverbs, and Job, distinguished by the Hebrew name, a word formed of the initial letters of these books, emeth, meaning truth. (2) Canticles, Ruth, Lamentations, Ecclesiastes, and Esther, called the five rolls, as being written for the synagogue use on five separate rolls. (3) Daniel, Ezra, Nehemiah, and 1 and 2 Chronicles. Between the Old and the New Testament no addition was made to the revelation God had already given. The period of New Testament revelation, extending over a century, began with the appearance of John the Baptist.
 The New Testament consists of (1) the historical books, viz., the Gospels, and the Acts of the Apostles; (2) the Epistles; and (3) the book of prophecy, the Revelation.
 The division of the Bible into chapters and verses is altogether of human invention, designed to facilitate reference to it. The ancient Jews divided the Old Testament into certain sections for use in the synagogue service, and then at a later period, in the ninth century A.D., into verses. Our modern system of chapters for all the books of the Bible was introduced by Cardinal Hugo about the middle of the thirteenth century (he died 1263). The system of verses for the New Testament was introduced by Stephens in 1551, and generally adopted, although neither Tyndale’s nor Coverdale’s English translation of the Bible has verses. The division is not always wisely made, yet it is very useful.
The frame on which dead bodies were conveyed to the grave (⟦42.7.14|눅 7:14⟧).
Garden, or gift of fortune, one of the seven eunuchs or chamberlains who had charge of the harem of Ahasuerus (⟦17.1.10|에 1:10⟧).

One of the eunuchs who “kept the door” in the court of Ahasuerus. With Teresh he conspired against the king’s life. Mordecai detected the conspiracy, and the culprits were hanged (⟦17.2.21|에 2:21⟧; ⟦17.6.1|6:1⟧).

Son of contention, one of Job’s friends. He is called “the Shuhite,” probably as belonging to Shuah, a district in Arabia, in which Shuah, the sixth son of Abraham by Keturah, settled (⟦1.25.2|창 25:2⟧). He took part in each of the three controversies into which Job’s friends entered with him (⟦18.8.1|욥 8:1⟧; ⟦18.18.1|18:1⟧; ⟦18.25.1|25:1⟧), and delivered three speeches, very severe and stern in their tone, although less violent than those of Zophar, but more so than those of Eliphaz.

Cheerful.
1. The head of the fifteenth sacerdotal course for the temple service (⟦13.24.14|대상 24:14⟧).
2. A priest who returned from Babylon with Zerubbabel (⟦16.12.5|느 12:5⟧, ⟦16.12.18|18⟧).

Faltering; bashful, Rachel’s handmaid, whom she gave to Jacob (⟦1.29.29|창 29:29⟧). She was the mother of Dan and Naphtali (⟦1.30.3|창 30:3⟧). Reuben was cursed by his father for committing adultry with her (35:22; 49:4). He was deprived of the birth-right, which was given to the sons of Joseph.
Son of the tongue; i.e., “eloquent”, a man of some note who returned from the Captivity with Zerubbabel (⟦15.2.2|스 2:2⟧; ⟦16.7.7|느 7:7⟧).

Birds are divided in the Mosaic law into two classes, (1) the clean (⟦3.1.14|레 1:14⟧; ⟦3.5.7|5:7⟧; ⟦3.14.4|14:4⟧), which were offered in sacrifice; and (2) the unclean (⟦3.11.13|레 11:13⟧). When offered in sacrifice, they were not divided as other victims were (⟦1.15.10|창 15:10⟧). They are mentioned also as an article of food (⟦5.14.11|신 14:11⟧). The art of snaring wild birds is referred to (⟦19.124.7|시 124:7⟧; ⟦20.1.17|잠 1:17⟧; ⟦20.7.23|7:23⟧; ⟦24.5.27|렘 5:27⟧). Singing birds are mentioned in ⟦19.104.12|시 104:12⟧; ⟦21.12.4|전 12:4⟧. Their timidity is alluded to (⟦28.11.11|호 11:11⟧). The reference in ⟦19.84.3|시 84:3⟧ to the swallow and the sparrow may be only a comparison equivalent to, “What her house is to the sparrow, and her nest to the swallow, that thine altars are to my soul.”
Son of wickedness, a king of Gomorrah whom Abraham succoured in the invasion of Chedorlaomer (⟦1.14.2|창 14:2⟧).

As soon as a child was born it was washed, and rubbed with salt (⟦26.16.4|겔 16:4⟧), and then swathed with bandages (⟦18.38.9|욥 38:9⟧; ⟦42.2.7|눅 2:7⟧, ⟦42.2.12|12⟧). A Hebrew mother remained forty days in seclusion after the birth of a son, and after the birth of a daughter double that number of days. At the close of that period she entered into the tabernacle or temple and offered up a sacrifice of purification (⟦3.12.1|레 12:1⟧; ⟦42.2.22|눅 2:22⟧). A son was circumcised on the eighth day after his birth, being thereby consecrated to God (⟦1.17.10|창 17:10⟧; comp. ⟦45.4.11|롬 4:11⟧). Seasons of misfortune are likened to the pains of a woman in travail, and seasons of prosperity to the joy that succeeds child-birth (⟦23.13.8|사 13:8⟧; ⟦24.4.31|렘 4:31⟧; ⟦43.16.21|요 16:21⟧, ⟦43.16.22|22⟧). The natural birth is referred to as the emblem of the new birth (⟦43.3.3|요 3:3⟧; ⟦48.6.15|갈 6:15⟧; ⟦56.3.5|딛 3:5⟧, etc.).

The observance of birth-days was common in early times (⟦18.1.4|욥 1:4⟧, ⟦18.1.13|13⟧, ⟦18.1.18|18⟧). They were specially celebrated in the land of Egypt (⟦1.40.20|창 40:20⟧). There is no recorded instance in Scripture of the celebration of birth-days among the Jews. On the occasion of Herod’s birth-day John the Baptist was beheaded (⟦40.14.6|마 14:6⟧).

1. This word denotes the special privileges and advantages belonging to the first-born son among the Jews. He became the priest of the family. Thus Reuben was the first-born of the patriarchs, and so the priesthood of the tribes belonged to him. That honour was, however, transferred by God from Reuben to Levi (⟦4.3.12|민 3:12⟧, ⟦4.3.13|13⟧; 8:18).
2. The first-born son had allotted to him also a double portion of the paternal inheritance (⟦5.21.15|신 21:15⟧). Reuben was, because of his undutiful conduct, deprived of his birth-right (⟦1.49.4|창 49:4⟧; ⟦13.5.1|대상 5:1⟧). Esau transferred his birth-right to Jacob (⟦1.25.33|창 25:33⟧).
3. The first-born inherited the judicial authority of his father, whatever it might be (⟦14.21.3|대하 21:3⟧). By divine appointment, however, David excluded Adonijah in favour of Solomon.
4. The Jews attached a sacred importance to the rank of “first-born” and “first-begotten” as applied to the Messiah (⟦45.8.29|롬 8:29⟧; ⟦51.1.18|골 1:18⟧; ⟦58.1.4|히 1:4⟧). As first-born he has an inheritance superior to his brethren, and is the alone true priest.

An overseer. In apostolic times, it is quite manifest that there was no difference as to order between bishops and elders or presbyters (⟦44.20.17|행 20:17⟧; ⟦60.5.1|벧전 5:1⟧, ⟦60.5.2|2⟧; ⟦50.1.1|빌 1:1⟧; ⟦54.3.1|딤전 3장⟧). The term bishop is never once used to denote a different office from that of elder or presbyter. These different names are simply titles of the same office, “bishop” designating the function, namely, that of oversight, and “presbyter” the dignity appertaining to the office. Christ is figuratively called “the bishop [episcopos] of souls” (⟦60.2.25|벧전 2:25⟧).

The curb put into the mouths of horses to restrain them. The Hebrew word (metheg) so rendered in ⟦19.32.9|시 32:9⟧ is elsewhere translated “bridle” (⟦12.19.28|왕하 19:28⟧; ⟦20.26.3|잠 26:3⟧; ⟦23.37.29|사 37:29⟧). Bits were generally made of bronze or iron, but sometimes also of gold or silver. In ⟦59.3.3|약 3:3⟧ the Authorized Version translates the Greek word by “bits,” but the Revised Version by “bridles.”

The broken or divided place, a district in the Arabah or Jordan valley, on the east of the river (⟦10.2.29|삼하 2:29⟧). It was probably the designation of the region in general, which is broken and intersected by ravines.

A province in Asia Minor, to the south of the Euxine and Propontis. Christian congregations were here formed at an early time (⟦60.1.1|벧전 1:1⟧). Paul was prevented by the Spirit from entering this province (⟦44.16.7|행 16:7⟧). It is noted in church history as the province ruled over by Pliny as Roman proconsul, who was perplexed as to the course he should take with the numerous Christians brought before his tribunal on account of their profession of Christianity and their conduct, and wrote to Trajan, the emperor, for instructions (A.D. 107).

Bitterness is symbolical of affliction, misery, and servitude (⟦2.1.14|출 1:14⟧; ⟦8.1.20|룻 1:20⟧; ⟦24.9.15|렘 9:15⟧). The Chaldeans are called the “bitter and hasty nation” (⟦35.1.6|합 1:6⟧). The “gall of bitterness” expresses a state of great wickedness (⟦44.8.23|행 8:23⟧). A “root of bitterness” is a wicked person or a dangerous sin (⟦58.12.15|히 12:15⟧).
 The Passover was to be eaten with “bitter herbs” (⟦2.12.8|출 12:8⟧; ⟦4.9.11|민 9:11⟧). The kind of herbs so designated is not known. Probably they were any bitter herbs obtainable at the place and time when the Passover was celebrated. They represented the severity of the servitude under which the people groaned; and have been regarded also as typical of the sufferings of Christ.

Is found three times in connection with the desolations to come upon Babylon, Idumea, and Nineveh (⟦23.14.23|사 14:23⟧; ⟦23.34.11|34:11⟧; ⟦36.2.14|습 2:14⟧). This bird belongs to the class of cranes. Its scientific name is Botaurus stellaris. It is a solitary bird, frequenting marshy ground. The Hebrew word (kippod) thus rendered in the Authorized Version is rendered “porcupine” in the Revised Version. But in the passages noted the kippod is associated with birds, with pools of water, and with solitude and desolation. This favours the idea that not the “porcupine” but the “bittern” is really intended by the word.
⟦1.11.3|창 11:3⟧, R.V., margin, rendered in the A.V. “slime”), a mineral pitch. With this the ark was pitched (6:14. See also ⟦2.2.3|출 2:3⟧.)

Properly the absence of all colour. In ⟦20.7.9|잠 7:9⟧ the Hebrew word means, as in the margin of the Revised Version, “the pupil of the eye.” It is translated “apple” of the eye in ⟦5.32.10|신 32:10⟧; ⟦19.17.8|시 17:8⟧; ⟦20.7.2|잠 7:2⟧. It is a different word which is rendered “black” in ⟦3.13.31|레 13:31⟧, ⟦3.13.37|37⟧; ⟦22.1.5|아 1:5⟧; ⟦22.5.11|5:11⟧; and ⟦38.6.2|슥 6:2⟧, ⟦38.6.6|6⟧. It is uncertain what the “black marble” of ⟦17.1.6|에 1:6⟧ was which formed a part of the mosaic pavement.

Applied to the glittering point of a spear (⟦18.39.23|욥 39:23⟧) or sword (⟦34.3.3|나 3:3⟧), the blade of a dagger (⟦7.3.22|삿 3:22⟧); the “shoulder blade” (⟦18.31.22|욥 31:22⟧); the “blade” of cereals (⟦40.13.26|마 13:26⟧).

Occurs only in connection with the sixth plague of Egypt (⟦2.9.9|출 9:9⟧, ⟦2.9.10|10⟧). In ⟦5.28.27|신 28:27⟧, ⟦5.28.35|35⟧, it is called “the botch of Egypt.” It seems to have been the fearful disease of black leprosy, a kind of elephantiasis, producing burning ulcers.

In the sense of speaking evil of God this word is found in ⟦19.74.18|시 74:18⟧; ⟦23.52.5|사 52:5⟧; ⟦45.2.24|롬 2:24⟧; ⟦66.13.1|계 13:1⟧, ⟦66.13.6|6⟧; 16:9, 11, 21. It denotes also any kind of calumny, or evil-speaking, or abuse (⟦11.21.10|왕상 21:10⟧; ⟦44.13.45|행 13:45⟧; ⟦44.18.6|18:6⟧, etc.). Our Lord was accused of blasphemy when he claimed to be the Son of God (⟦40.26.65|마 26:65⟧; comp. ⟦40.9.3|마 9:3⟧; ⟦41.2.7|막 2:7⟧). They who deny his Messiahship blaspheme Jesus (⟦42.22.65|눅 22:65⟧; ⟦43.10.36|요 10:36⟧).
 Blasphemy against the Holy Ghost (⟦40.12.31|마 12:31⟧, ⟦40.12.32|32⟧; ⟦41.3.28|막 3:28⟧, ⟦41.3.29|29⟧; ⟦42.12.10|눅 12:10⟧) is regarded by some as a continued and obstinate rejection of the gospel, and hence is an unpardonable sin, simply because as long as a sinner remains in unbelief he voluntarily excludes himself from pardon. Others regard the expression as designating the sin of attributing to the power of Satan those miracles which Christ performed, or generally those works which are the result of the Spirit’s agency.
Chamberlain to king Herod Agrippa I. (⟦44.12.20|행 12:20⟧). Such persons generally had great influence with their masters.

Imperfection or bodily deformity excluding men from the priesthood, and rendering animals unfit to be offered in sacrifice (⟦3.21.17|레 21:17⟧; ⟦3.22.19|22:19⟧). The Christian church, as justified in Christ, is “without blemish” (⟦49.5.27|엡 5:27⟧). Christ offered himself a sacrifice “without blemish,” acceptable to God (⟦60.1.19|벧전 1:19⟧).

1. God blesses his people when he bestows on them some gift temporal or spiritual (⟦1.1.22|창 1:22⟧; ⟦1.24.35|24:35⟧; ⟦18.42.12|욥 42:12⟧; ⟦19.45.2|시 45:2⟧; ⟦19.104.24|104:24⟧, ⟦19.104.35|35⟧).
2. We bless God when we thank him for his mercies (⟦19.103.1|시 103:1⟧, ⟦19.103.2|2⟧; ⟦19.145.1|145:1⟧, ⟦19.145.2|2⟧).
3. A man blesses himself when he invokes God’s blessing (⟦23.65.16|사 65:16⟧), or rejoices in God’s goodness to him (⟦5.29.19|신 29:19⟧; ⟦19.49.18|시 49:18⟧).
4. One blesses another when he expresses good wishes or offers prayer to God for his welfare (⟦1.24.60|창 24:60⟧; ⟦1.31.55|31:55⟧; ⟦9.2.20|삼상 2:20⟧). Sometimes blessings were uttered under divine inspiration, as in the case of Noah, Isaac, Jacob, and Moses (⟦1.9.26|창 9:26⟧, ⟦1.9.27|27⟧; 27:28, 29, 40; 48:15-20; 49:1-28; ⟦5.33.1|신 33장⟧). The priests were divinely authorized to bless the people (⟦5.10.8|신 10:8⟧; ⟦4.6.22|민 6:22⟧). We have many examples of apostolic benediction (⟦47.13.13|고후 13:13⟧; ⟦49.6.23|엡 6:23⟧, ⟦49.6.24|24⟧; ⟦53.3.16|살후 3:16⟧, ⟦53.3.18|18⟧; ⟦58.13.20|히 13:20⟧, ⟦58.13.21|21⟧; ⟦60.5.10|벧전 5:10⟧, ⟦60.5.11|11⟧).
5. Among the Jews in their thank-offerings the master of the feast took a cup of wine in his hand, and after having blessed God for it and for other mercies then enjoyed, handed it to his guests, who all partook of it. ⟦19.116.13|시 116:13⟧ refers to this custom. It is also alluded to in ⟦46.10.16|고전 10:16⟧, where the apostle speaks of the “cup of blessing.”

Blind beggars are frequently mentioned (⟦40.9.27|마 9:27⟧; ⟦40.12.22|12:22⟧; ⟦40.20.30|20:30⟧; ⟦43.5.3|요 5:3⟧). The blind are to be treated with compassion (⟦3.19.14|레 19:14⟧; ⟦5.27.18|신 27:18⟧). Blindness was sometimes a punishment for disobedience (⟦9.11.2|삼상 11:2⟧; ⟦24.39.7|렘 39:7⟧), sometimes the effect of old age (⟦1.27.1|창 27:1⟧; ⟦11.14.4|왕상 14:4⟧; ⟦9.4.15|삼상 4:15⟧). Conquerors sometimes blinded their captives (⟦12.25.7|왕하 25:7⟧; ⟦9.11.2|삼상 11:2⟧). Blindness denotes ignorance as to spiritual things (⟦23.6.10|사 6:10⟧; ⟦23.42.18|42:18⟧, ⟦23.42.19|19⟧; ⟦40.15.14|마 15:14⟧; ⟦49.4.18|엡 4:18⟧). The opening of the eyes of the blind is peculiar to the Messiah (⟦23.29.18|사 29:18⟧). Elymas was smitten with blindness at Paul’s word (⟦44.13.11|행 13:11⟧).

1. As food, prohibited in ⟦1.9.4|창 9:4⟧, where the use of animal food is first allowed. Comp. ⟦5.12.23|신 12:23⟧; ⟦3.3.17|레 3:17⟧; ⟦3.7.26|7:26⟧; ⟦3.17.10|17:10⟧. The injunction to abstain from blood is renewed in the decree of the council of Jerusalem (⟦44.15.29|행 15:29⟧). It has been held by some, and we think correctly, that this law of prohibition was only ceremonial and temporary; while others regard it as still binding on all. Blood was eaten by the Israelites after the battle of Gilboa (⟦9.14.32|삼상 14:32⟧).
2. The blood of sacrifices was caught by the priest in a basin, and then sprinkled seven times on the altar; that of the passover on the doorposts and lintels of the houses (⟦2.12.1|출 12장⟧; ⟦3.4.5|레 4:5⟧; ⟦3.16.14|16:14⟧). At the giving of the law (⟦2.24.8|출 24:8⟧) the blood of the sacrifices was sprinkled on the people as well as on the altar, and thus the people were consecrated to God, or entered into covenant with him, hence the blood of the covenant (⟦40.26.28|마 26:28⟧; ⟦58.9.19|히 9:19⟧, ⟦58.9.20|20⟧; 10:29; 13:20).
3. Human blood. The murderer was to be punished (⟦1.9.5|창 9:5⟧). The blood of the murdered “crieth for vengeance” (⟦1.4.10|창 4:10⟧). The “avenger of blood” was the nearest relative of the murdered, and he was required to avenge his death (⟦4.35.24|민 35:24⟧, ⟦4.35.27|27⟧). No satisfaction could be made for the guilt of murder (⟦4.35.31|민 35:31⟧).
4. Blood used metaphorically to denote race (⟦44.17.26|행 17:26⟧), and as a symbol of slaughter (⟦23.34.3|사 34:3⟧). To “wash the feet in blood” means to gain a great victory (⟦19.58.10|시 58:10⟧). Wine, from its red colour, is called “the blood of the grape” (⟦1.49.11|창 49:11⟧). Blood and water issued from our Saviour’s side when it was pierced by the Roman soldier (⟦43.19.34|요 19:34⟧). This has led pathologists to the conclusion that the proper cause of Christ’s death was rupture of the heart. (Comp. ⟦19.69.20|시 69:20⟧.)
The sign and token of our Lord’s great agony (⟦42.22.44|눅 22:44⟧).

A stain or reproach (⟦18.31.7|욥 31:7⟧; ⟦20.9.7|잠 9:7⟧). To blot out sin is to forgive it (⟦19.51.1|시 51:1⟧, ⟦19.51.9|9⟧; ⟦23.44.22|사 44:22⟧; ⟦44.3.19|행 3:19⟧). Christ’s blotting out the handwriting of ordinances was his fulfilling the law in our behalf (⟦51.2.14|골 2:14⟧).

Generally associated with purple (⟦2.25.4|출 25:4⟧; ⟦2.26.1|26:1⟧, ⟦2.26.31|31⟧, ⟦2.26.36|36⟧, etc.). It is supposed to have been obtained from a shellfish of the Mediterranean, the Helix ianthina of Linnaeus. The robe of the high priest’s ephod was to be all of this colour (⟦2.28.31|출 28:31⟧), also the loops of the curtains (26:4) and the ribbon of the breastplate (28:28). Blue cloths were also made for various sacred purposes (⟦4.4.6|민 4:6⟧, ⟦4.4.7|7⟧, ⟦4.4.9|9⟧, ⟦4.4.11|11⟧, ⟦4.4.12|12⟧).
Sons of thunder, a surname given by our Lord to James and John (⟦41.3.17|막 3:17⟧) on account of their fervid and impetuous temper (⟦42.9.54|눅 9:54⟧).

Occurs only in ⟦19.80.13|시 80:13⟧. The same Hebrew word is elsewhere rendered “swine” (⟦3.11.7|레 11:7⟧; ⟦5.14.8|신 14:8⟧; ⟦20.11.22|잠 11:22⟧; ⟦23.65.4|사 65:4⟧; ⟦23.66.3|66:3⟧, ⟦23.66.17|17⟧). The Hebrews abhorred swine’s flesh, and accordingly none of these animals were reared, except in the district beyond the Sea of Galilee. In the psalm quoted above the powers that destroyed the Jewish nation are compared to wild boars and wild beasts of the field.

Alacrity.
1. The husband of Ruth, a wealthy Bethlehemite. By the “levirate law” the duty devolved on him of marrying Ruth the Moabitess (⟦8.4.1|룻 4:1⟧). He was a kinsman of Mahlon, her first husband.
2. The name given (for what reason is unknown) to one of the two (the other was called Jachin) brazen pillars which Solomon erected in the court of the temple (⟦11.7.21|왕상 7:21⟧; ⟦14.3.17|대하 3:17⟧). These pillars were broken up and carried to Babylon by Nebuchadnezzar.

Weepers, a place where the angel of the Lord reproved the Israelites for entering into a league with the people of the land. This caused them bitterly to weep, and hence the name of the place (⟦7.2.1|삿 2:1⟧, ⟦7.2.5|5⟧). It lay probably at the head of one of the valleys between Gilgal and Shiloh.

(rendered “botch” in ⟦5.28.27|신 28:27⟧, ⟦5.28.35|35⟧), an aggravated ulcer, as in the case of Hezekiah (⟦12.20.7|왕하 20:7⟧; ⟦23.38.21|사 38:21⟧) or of the Egyptians (⟦2.9.9|출 9:9⟧, ⟦2.9.10|10⟧, ⟦2.9.11|11⟧; ⟦5.28.27|신 28:27⟧, ⟦5.28.35|35⟧). It designates the disease of Job (2:7), which was probably the black leprosy.

(⟦2.9.31|출 9:31⟧), meaning “swollen or podded for seed,” was adopted in the Authorized Version from the version of Coverdale (1535). The Revised Version has in the margin “was in bloom,” which is the more probable rendering of the Hebrew word. It is the fact that in Egypt when barley is in ear (about February) flax is blossoming.

The Hebrew word kebir, rendered “pillow” in ⟦9.19.13|삼상 19:13⟧, ⟦9.19.16|16⟧, but in Revised Version marg. “quilt” or “network,” probably means some counterpane or veil intended to protect the head of the sleeper. A different Hebrew word (meraashoth’) is used for “bolster” (⟦9.26.7|삼상 26:7⟧, ⟦9.26.11|11⟧, ⟦9.26.16|16⟧). It is rightly rendered in Revised Version “at his head.” In ⟦1.28.11|창 28:11⟧, ⟦1.28.18|18⟧ the Authorized Version renders it “for his pillows,” and the Revised Version “under his head.” In ⟦26.13.18|겔 13:18⟧, ⟦26.13.20|20⟧ another Hebrew word (kesathoth) is used, properly denoting “cushions” or “pillows,” as so rendered both in the Authorized and the Revised Version.

An obligation of any kind (⟦4.30.2|민 30:2⟧, ⟦4.30.4|4⟧, ⟦4.30.12|12⟧). The word means also oppression or affliction (⟦19.116.16|시 116:16⟧; ⟦50.1.7|빌 1:7⟧). Christian love is the “bond of perfectness” (⟦51.3.14|골 3:14⟧), and the influences of the Spirit are the “bond of peace” (⟦49.4.3|엡 4:3⟧).

Of Israel in Egypt (⟦2.2.23|출 2:23⟧, ⟦2.2.25|25⟧; 5), which is called the “house of bondage” (13:3; 20:2). This word is used also with reference to the captivity in Babylon (⟦23.14.3|사 14:3⟧), and the oppression of the Persian king (⟦15.9.8|스 9:8⟧, ⟦15.9.9|9⟧).

(Heb. peer), ⟦2.39.28|출 39:28⟧ (R.V., “head-tires”); ⟦26.44.18|겔 44:18⟧ (R.V., “tires”), denotes properly a turban worn by priests, and in ⟦23.3.20|사 3:20⟧ (R.V., “head-tires”) a head-dress or tiara worn by females. The Hebrew word so rendered literally means an ornament, as in ⟦23.61.10|사 61:10⟧ (R.V., “garland”), and in ⟦26.24.17|겔 24:17⟧, ⟦26.24.23|23⟧ “tire” (R.V., “head-tire”). It consisted of a piece of cloth twisted about the head. In ⟦2.28.40|출 28:40⟧; ⟦2.29.9|29:9⟧ it is the translation of a different Hebrew word (migba’ah), which denotes the turban (R.V., “head-tire”) of the common priest as distinguished from the mitre of the high priest.

This word has a comprehensive meaning in Scripture. In the Old Testament it is the rendering of the Hebrew word sepher, which properly means a “writing,” and then a “volume” (⟦2.17.14|출 17:14⟧; ⟦5.28.58|신 28:58⟧; ⟦5.29.20|29:20⟧; ⟦18.19.23|욥 19:23⟧) or “roll of a book” (⟦24.36.2|렘 36:2⟧, ⟦24.36.4|4⟧).
 Books were originally written on skins, on linen or cotton cloth, and on Egyptian papyrus, whence our word “paper.” The leaves of the book were generally written in columns, designated by a Hebrew word properly meaning “doors” and “valves” (⟦24.36.23|렘 36:23⟧, R.V., marg. “columns”).
 Among the Hebrews books were generally rolled up like our maps, or if very long they were rolled from both ends, forming two rolls (⟦42.4.17|눅 4:17⟧). Thus they were arranged when the writing was on flexible materials; but if the writing was on tablets of wood or brass or lead, then the several tablets were bound together by rings through which a rod was passed.
 A sealed book is one whose contents are secret (⟦23.29.11|사 29:11⟧; ⟦66.5.1|계 5:1⟧). To “eat” a book (⟦24.15.16|렘 15:16⟧; ⟦26.2.8|겔 2:8⟧; ⟦26.3.1|3:1⟧; ⟦66.10.9|계 10:9⟧) is to study its contents carefully.
 The book of judgment (⟦27.7.10|단 7:10⟧) refers to the method of human courts of justice as illustrating the proceedings which will take place at the day of God’s final judgment.
 The book of the wars of the Lord (⟦4.21.14|민 21:14⟧), the book of Jasher (⟦6.10.13|수 10:13⟧), and the book of the chronicles of the kings of Judah and Israel (⟦14.25.26|대하 25:26⟧), were probably ancient documents known to the Hebrews, but not forming a part of the canon.
 The book of life (⟦19.69.28|시 69:28⟧) suggests the idea that as the redeemed form a community or citizenship (⟦50.3.20|빌 3:20⟧; ⟦50.4.3|4:3⟧), a catalogue of the citizens’ names is preserved (⟦42.10.20|눅 10:20⟧; ⟦66.20.15|계 20:15⟧). Their names are registered in heaven (⟦42.10.20|눅 10:20⟧; ⟦66.3.5|계 3:5⟧).
 The book of the covenant (⟦2.24.7|출 24:7⟧), containing ⟦2.20.22|출 20:22⟧, is the first book actually mentioned as a part of the written word. It contains a series of laws, civil, social, and religious, given to Moses at Sinai immediately after the delivery of the decalogue. These were written in this “book.”

A hut made of the branches of a tree. In such tabernacles Jacob sojourned for a season at a place named from this circumstance Succoth (⟦1.33.17|창 33:17⟧). Booths were erected also at the feast of Tabernacles (q.v.), ⟦3.23.42|레 23:42⟧, ⟦3.23.43|43⟧, which commemorated the abode of the Israelites in the wilderness.

Captives or cattle or objects of value taken in war. In Canaan all that breathed were to be destroyed (⟦5.20.1|신 20장⟧: 16). The “pictures and images” of the Canaanites were to be destroyed also (⟦4.33.52|민 33:52⟧). The law of booty as to its division is laid down in ⟦4.31.26|민 31:26⟧. David afterwards introduced a regulation that the baggage-guard should share the booty equally with the soldiers engaged in battle. He also devoted of the spoils of war for the temple (⟦9.30.24|삼상 30:24⟧; ⟦10.8.11|삼하 8:11⟧; ⟦13.26.27|대상 26:27⟧).

The Israelites “borrowed” from the Egyptians (⟦2.12.35|출 12:35⟧, R.V., “asked”) in accordance with a divine command (3:22; 11:2). But the word (sha’al) so rendered here means simply and always to “request” or “demand.” The Hebrew had another word which is properly translated “borrow” in ⟦5.28.12|신 28:12⟧; ⟦19.37.21|시 37:21⟧. It was well known that the parting was final. The Egyptians were so anxious to get the Israelites away out of their land that “they let them have what they asked” (⟦2.12.36|출 12:36⟧, R.V.), or literally “made them to ask,” urged them to take whatever they desired and depart.

In the East objects are carried in the bosom which Europeans carry in the pocket. To have in one’s bosom indicates kindness, secrecy, or intimacy (⟦1.16.5|창 16:5⟧; ⟦10.12.8|삼하 12:8⟧). Christ is said to have been in “the bosom of the Father,” i.e., he had the most perfect knowledge of the Father, had the closest intimacy with him (⟦43.1.18|요 1:18⟧). John (13:23) was “leaning on Jesus’ bosom” at the last supper. Our Lord carries his lambs in his bosom, i.e., has a tender, watchful care over them (⟦23.40.11|사 40:11⟧).
The Chaldee or Aramaic form of the name Beor, the father of Balaam (2 Pet. 2:15).
The projecting parts of a shield (⟦18.15.26|욥 15:26⟧). The Hebrew word thus rendered means anything convex or arched, and hence the back, as of animals.
The name given in ⟦5.28.27|신 28:27⟧, ⟦5.28.35|35⟧ to one of the Egyptian plagues (⟦2.9.9|출 9:9⟧). The word so translated is usually rendered “boil” (q.v.).

A vessel made of skins for holding wine (⟦6.9.4|수 9:4⟧. 13; ⟦9.16.20|삼상 16:20⟧; ⟦40.9.17|마 9:17⟧; ⟦41.2.22|막 2:22⟧; ⟦42.5.37|눅 5:37⟧, ⟦42.5.38|38⟧), or milk (⟦7.4.19|삿 4:19⟧), or water (⟦1.21.14|창 21:14⟧, ⟦1.21.15|15⟧, ⟦1.21.19|19⟧), or strong drink (⟦35.2.15|합 2:15⟧).
 Earthenware vessels were also similarly used (⟦24.19.1|렘 19:1⟧; ⟦11.14.3|왕상 14:3⟧; ⟦23.30.14|사 30:14⟧). In ⟦18.32.19|욥 32:19⟧ (comp. ⟦40.9.17|마 9:17⟧; ⟦42.5.37|눅 5:37⟧, ⟦42.5.38|38⟧; ⟦41.2.22|막 2:22⟧) the reference is to a wine-skin ready to burst through the fermentation of the wine. “Bottles of wine” in the Authorized Version of ⟦28.7.5|호 7:5⟧ is properly rendered in the Revised Version by “the heat of wine,” i.e., the fever of wine, its intoxicating strength.
 The clouds are figuratively called the “bottles of heaven” (⟦18.38.37|욥 38:37⟧). A bottle blackened or shrivelled by smoke is referred to in ⟦19.119.83|시 119:83⟧ as an image to which the psalmist likens himself.

The bow was in use in early times both in war and in the chase (⟦1.21.20|창 21:20⟧; ⟦1.27.3|27:3⟧; ⟦1.48.22|48:22⟧). The tribe of Benjamin were famous for the use of the bow (⟦13.8.40|대상 8:40⟧; ⟦13.12.2|12:2⟧; ⟦14.14.8|대하 14:8⟧; ⟦14.17.17|17:17⟧); so also were the Elamites (⟦23.22.6|사 22:6⟧) and the Lydians (⟦24.46.9|렘 46:9⟧). The Hebrew word commonly used for bow means properly to tread (⟦13.5.18|대상 5:18⟧; ⟦13.8.40|8:40⟧), and hence it is concluded that the foot was employed in bending the bow. Bows of steel (correctly “copper”) are mentioned (⟦10.22.35|삼하 22:35⟧; ⟦19.18.34|시 18:34⟧).
 The arrows were carried in a quiver (⟦1.27.3|창 27:3⟧; ⟦23.22.6|사 22:6⟧; ⟦23.49.2|49:2⟧; ⟦19.127.5|시 127:5⟧). They were apparently sometimes shot with some burning material attached to them (⟦19.120.4|시 120:4⟧).
 The bow is a symbol of victory (⟦19.7.12|시 7:12⟧). It denotes also falsehood, deceit (⟦19.64.3|시 64:3⟧, ⟦19.64.4|4⟧; ⟦28.7.16|호 7:16⟧; ⟦24.9.3|렘 9:3⟧).
 “The use of the bow” in ⟦10.1.18|삼하 1:18⟧ (A.V.) ought to be “the song of the bow,” as in the Revised Version.

A mode of showing respect. Abraham “bowed himself to the people of the land” (⟦1.23.7|창 23:7⟧); so Jacob to Esau (⟦1.33.3|창 33:3⟧); and the brethren of Joseph before him as the governor of the land (⟦1.43.28|창 43:28⟧). Bowing is also frequently mentioned as an act of adoration to idols (⟦6.23.7|수 23:7⟧; ⟦12.5.18|왕하 5:18⟧; ⟦7.2.19|삿 2:19⟧; ⟦23.44.15|사 44:15⟧), and to God (⟦6.5.14|수 5:14⟧; ⟦19.22.29|시 22:29⟧; ⟦19.72.9|72:9⟧; ⟦33.6.6|미 6:6⟧; ⟦19.95.6|시 95:6⟧; ⟦49.3.14|엡 3:14⟧).

The sockets of the lamps of the golden candlestick of the tabernacle are called bowls (⟦2.25.31|출 25:31⟧, ⟦2.25.33|33⟧, ⟦2.25.34|34⟧; 37:17, 19, 20); the same word so rendered being elsewhere rendered “cup” (⟦1.44.2|창 44:2⟧, ⟦1.44.12|12⟧, ⟦1.44.16|16⟧), and wine “pot” (⟦24.35.5|렘 35:5⟧). The reservoir for oil, from which pipes led to each lamp in Zechariah’s vision of the candlestick, is called also by this name (⟦38.4.2|슥 4:2⟧, ⟦38.4.3|3⟧); so also are the vessels used for libations (⟦2.25.29|출 25:29⟧; ⟦2.37.16|37:16⟧).

For holding oil or perfumery (⟦41.14.3|막 14:3⟧). It was of the form of a flask or bottle. The Hebrew word (pak) used for it is more appropriately rendered “vial” in ⟦9.10.1|삼상 10:1⟧, and should also be so rendered in ⟦12.9.1|왕하 9:1⟧, where alone else it occurs.

(Heb. teashshur), mentioned in ⟦23.60.13|사 60:13⟧; ⟦23.41.19|41:19⟧, was, according to some, a species of cedar growing in Lebanon. The words of ⟦26.27.6|겔 27:6⟧ literally translated are, “Thy benches they have made of ivory, the daughter of the ashur tree,” i.e., inlaid with ashur wood. The ashur is the box-tree, and accordingly the Revised Version rightly reads “inlaid in box wood.” This is the Buxus sempervirens of botanists. It is remarkable for the beauty of its evergreen foliage and for the utility of its hard and durable wood.

Enclosure; fortress.
1. The city of Jobab, one of the early Edomite kings (⟦1.36.33|창 36:33⟧). This place is mentioned by the prophets in later times (⟦23.34.6|사 34:6⟧; ⟦24.49.13|렘 49:13⟧; ⟦30.1.12|암 1:12⟧; ⟦33.2.12|미 2:12⟧). Its modern representative is el-Busseireh. It lies in the mountain district of Petra, 20 miles to the south-east of the Dead Sea.
2. A Moabite city in the “plain country” (⟦24.48.24|렘 48:24⟧), i.e., on the high level down on the east of the Dead Sea. It is probably the modern Buzrah.

1. Anklets (⟦4.31.50|민 31:50⟧; ⟦10.1.10|삼하 1:10⟧), and with reference to men.
2. The rendering of a Hebrew word meaning fasteners, found in ⟦1.24.22|창 24:22⟧, ⟦1.24.30|30⟧, ⟦1.24.47|47⟧.
3. In ⟦23.3.19|사 3:19⟧, the rendering of a Hebrew word meaning chains, i.e., twisted or chain-like bracelets.
4. In ⟦2.35.22|출 35:22⟧ it designates properly a clasp for fastening the dress of females. Some interpret it as a nose-ring.
5. In ⟦1.38.18|창 38:18⟧, ⟦1.38.25|25⟧, the rendering of a Hebrew word meaning “thread,” and may denote the ornamental cord with which the signet was suspended from the neck of the wearer.
 Bracelets were worn by men as well as by women (⟦22.5.14|아 5:14⟧, R.V.). They were of many various forms. The weight of those presented by Eliezer to Rebekah was ten shekels (⟦1.24.22|창 24:22⟧).

1. Hebrew atad, ⟦7.9.14|삿 9:14⟧; rendered “thorn,” ⟦19.58.9|시 58:9⟧. The LXX. and Vulgate render by rhamnus, a thorny shrub common in Palestine, resembling the hawthorn.
2. Hebrew hoah, ⟦23.34.13|사 34:13⟧ (R.V. “thistles”); “thickets” in ⟦9.13.6|삼상 13:6⟧; “thistles” in ⟦12.14.9|왕하 14:9⟧, ⟦12.14.2|2⟧ Chr. 25:18, ⟦18.31.40|욥 31:40⟧; “thorns” in ⟦14.33.11|대하 33:11⟧, ⟦22.2.2|아 2:2⟧, ⟦28.9.6|호 9:6⟧. The word may be regarded as denoting the common thistle, of which there are many species which encumber the corn-fields of Palestine.

A symbol of kings descended from royal ancestors (⟦26.17.3|겔 17:3⟧, ⟦26.17.10|10⟧; ⟦27.11.7|단 11:7⟧); of prosperity (⟦18.8.16|욥 8:16⟧); of the Messiah, a branch out of the root of the stem of Jesse (⟦23.11.1|사 11:1⟧), the “beautiful branch” (4:2), a “righteous branch” (⟦24.23.5|렘 23:5⟧), “the Branch” (⟦38.3.8|슥 3:8⟧; ⟦38.6.12|6:12⟧).
 Disciples are branches of the true vine (⟦43.15.5|요 15:5⟧, ⟦43.15.6|6⟧). “The branch of the terrible ones” (⟦23.25.5|사 25:5⟧) is rightly translated in the Revised Version “the song of the terrible ones,” i.e., the song of victory shall be brought low by the destruction of Babylon and the return of the Jews from captivity.
 The “abominable branch” is a tree on which a malefactor has been hanged (⟦23.14.19|사 14:19⟧). The “highest branch” in ⟦26.17.3|겔 17:3⟧ represents Jehoiakim the king.

Which is an alloy of copper and zinc, was not known till the thirteenth century. What is designated by this word in Scripture is properly copper (⟦5.8.9|신 8:9⟧). It was used for fetters (⟦7.16.21|삿 16:21⟧; ⟦12.25.7|왕하 25:7⟧), for pieces of armour (⟦9.17.5|삼상 17:5⟧, ⟦9.17.6|6⟧), for musical instruments (⟦13.15.19|대상 15:19⟧; ⟦46.13.1|고전 13:1⟧), and for money (⟦40.10.9|마 10:9⟧).
 It is a symbol of insensibility and obstinacy in sin (⟦23.48.4|사 48:4⟧; ⟦24.6.28|렘 6:28⟧; ⟦26.22.18|겔 22:18⟧), and of strength (⟦19.107.16|시 107:16⟧; ⟦33.4.13|미 4:13⟧).
 The Macedonian empire is described as a kingdom of brass (⟦27.2.39|단 2:39⟧). The “mountains of brass” Zechariah (6:1) speaks of have been supposed to represent the immutable decrees of God.
 The serpent of brass was made by Moses at the command of God (⟦4.21.4|민 21:4⟧), and elevated on a pole, so that it might be seen by all the people when wounded by the bite of the serpents that were sent to them as a punishment for their murmurings against God and against Moses. It was afterwards carried by the Jews into Canaan, and preserved by them till the time of Hezekiah, who caused it to be at length destroyed because it began to be viewed by the people with superstitious reverence (⟦12.18.4|왕하 18:4⟧).
 The brazen serpent is alluded to by our Lord in ⟦43.3.14|요 3:14⟧, ⟦43.3.15|15⟧.
(⟦23.3.18|사 3:18⟧), an old English word meaning comeliness or beauty.

An opening in a wall (⟦11.11.27|왕상 11:27⟧; ⟦12.12.5|왕하 12:5⟧); the fracture of a limb (⟦3.24.20|레 24:20⟧), and hence the expression, “Heal, etc.” (⟦19.60.2|시 60:2⟧). ⟦7.5.17|삿 5:17⟧, a bay or harbour; R.V., “by his creeks.”

Among the Jews was generally made of wheat (⟦2.29.2|출 29:2⟧; ⟦7.6.19|삿 6:19⟧), though also sometimes of other grains (⟦1.14.18|창 14:18⟧; ⟦7.7.13|삿 7:13⟧). Parched grain was sometimes used for food without any other preparation (⟦8.2.14|룻 2:14⟧).
 Bread was prepared by kneading in wooden bowls or “kneading troughs” (⟦1.18.6|창 18:6⟧; ⟦2.12.34|출 12:34⟧; ⟦24.7.18|렘 7:18⟧). The dough was mixed with leaven and made into thin cakes, round or oval, and then baked. The bread eaten at the Passover was always unleavened (⟦2.12.15|출 12:15⟧; ⟦5.16.3|신 16:3⟧). In the towns there were public ovens, which were much made use of for baking bread; there were also bakers by trade (⟦28.7.4|호 7:4⟧; ⟦24.37.21|렘 37:21⟧). Their ovens were not unlike those of modern times. But sometimes the bread was baked by being placed on the ground that had been heated by a fire, and by covering it with the embers (⟦11.19.6|왕상 19:6⟧). This was probably the mode in which Sarah prepared bread on the occasion referred to in ⟦1.18.6|창 18:6⟧.
 In ⟦3.2.1|레 2장⟧ there is an account of the different kinds of bread and cakes used by the Jews.
 The shew-bread (q.v.) consisted of twelve loaves of unleavened bread prepared and presented hot on the golden table every Sabbath. They were square or oblong, and represented the twelve tribes of Israel. The old loaves were removed every Sabbath, and were to be eaten only by the priests in the court of the sanctuary (⟦2.25.30|출 25:30⟧; ⟦3.24.8|레 24:8⟧; ⟦9.21.1|삼상 21:1⟧; ⟦40.12.4|마 12:4⟧).
 The word bread is used figuratively in such expressions as “bread of sorrows” (⟦19.127.2|시 127:2⟧), “bread of tears” (80:5), i.e., sorrow and tears are like one’s daily bread, they form so great a part in life. The bread of “wickedness” (⟦20.4.17|잠 4:17⟧) and “of deceit” (20:17) denote in like manner that wickedness and deceit are a part of the daily life.

1. That piece of ancient armour that protected the breast. This word is used figuratively in ⟦49.6.14|엡 6:14⟧ and ⟦23.59.17|사 59:17⟧.
2. An ornament covering the breast of the high priest, first mentioned in ⟦2.25.7|출 25:7⟧. It was made of embroidered cloth, set with four rows of precious stones, three in each row. On each stone was engraved the name of one of the twelve tribes (⟦2.28.15|출 28:15⟧; ⟦2.39.8|39:8⟧). It was in size about ten inches square. The two upper corners were fastened to the ephod by blue ribbons. It was not to be “loosed from the ephod” (⟦2.28.28|출 28:28⟧). The lower corners were fastened to the girdle of the priest. As it reminded the priest of his representative character, it was called the memorial (28:29). It was also called the breastplate of judgment (28:15).
(⟦2.28.42|출 28:42⟧), rather linen drawers, reaching from the waist to a little above the knee, worn by the priests (⟦26.44.17|겔 44:17⟧, ⟦26.44.18|18⟧).
None to be taken; “for the gift maketh open eyes blind, and perverteth the cause of the righteous” (⟦2.23.8|출 23:8⟧, literally rendered).

The making of, formed the chief labour of the Israelites in Egypt (⟦2.1.13|출 1:13⟧, ⟦2.1.14|14⟧). Those found among the ruins of Babylon and Nineveh are about a foot square and four inches thick. They were usually dried in the sun, though also sometimes in kilns (⟦10.12.31|삼하 12:31⟧; ⟦24.43.9|렘 43:9⟧; ⟦34.3.14|나 3:14⟧).
 The bricks used in the tower of Babel were burnt bricks, cemented in the building by bitumen (⟦1.11.3|창 11:3⟧).

Frequently used in the ordinary sense (⟦23.49.18|사 49:18⟧; ⟦23.61.10|61:10⟧, etc.). The relation between Christ and his church is set forth under the figure of that between a bridegroom and bride (⟦43.3.29|요 3:29⟧). The church is called “the bride” (⟦66.21.9|계 21:9⟧; ⟦66.22.17|22:17⟧). Compare parable of the Ten Virgins (⟦40.25.1|마 25:1⟧).

Three Hebrew words are thus rendered in the Authorized Version.
1. Heb. mahsom’ signifies a muzzle or halter or bridle, by which the rider governs his horse (⟦19.39.1|시 39:1⟧).
2. Me’theg, rendered also “bit” in ⟦19.32.9|시 32:9⟧, which is its proper meaning. Found in ⟦12.19.28|왕하 19:28⟧, where the restraints of God’s providence are metaphorically styled his “bridle” and “hook.” God’s placing a “bridle in the jaws of the people” (⟦23.30.28|사 30:28⟧; ⟦23.37.29|37:29⟧) signifies his preventing the Assyrians from carrying out their purpose against Jerusalem.
3. Another word, re’sen, was employed to represent a halter or bridle-rein, as used ⟦19.32.9|시 32:9⟧; ⟦23.30.28|사 30:28⟧. In ⟦18.30.11|욥 30:11⟧ the restraints of law and humanity are called a bridle.

This word occurs frequently, and is the translation of several different terms.
1. ⟦33.7.4|미 7:4⟧, it denotes a species of thorn shrub used for hedges. In ⟦20.15.19|잠 15:19⟧ the word is rendered “thorn” (Heb. hedek, “stinging”), supposed by some to be what is called the “apple of Sodom” (q.v.).
2. ⟦26.28.24|겔 28:24⟧, sallon’, properly a “prickle,” such as is found on the shoots of the palm tree.
3. ⟦23.55.13|사 55:13⟧, probably simply a thorny bush. Some, following the Vulgate Version, regard it as the “nettle.”
4. ⟦23.5.6|사 5:6⟧; ⟦23.7.23|7:23⟧, etc., frequently used to denote thorny shrubs in general. In 10:17; 27:4, it means troublesome men.
5. In ⟦58.6.8|히 6:8⟧ the Greek word (tribolos) so rendered means “three-pronged,” and denotes the land caltrop, a low throny shrub resembling in its spikes the military “crow-foot.” Comp. ⟦40.7.16|마 7:16⟧, “thistle.”
(⟦24.46.4|렘 46:4⟧; ⟦24.51.3|51:3⟧), an obsolete English word denoting a scale coat of armour, or habergeon, worn by light-armed “brigands.” The Revised Version has “coat of mail.”

An inflammable mineral substance found in quantities on the shores of the Dead Sea. The cities of the plain were destroyed by a rain of fire and brimstone (⟦1.19.24|창 19:24⟧, ⟦1.19.25|25⟧). In ⟦23.34.9|사 34:9⟧ allusion is made to the destruction of these cities. This word figuratively denotes destruction or punishment (⟦18.18.15|욥 18:15⟧; ⟦23.30.33|사 30:33⟧; ⟦23.34.9|34:9⟧; ⟦19.11.6|시 11:6⟧; ⟦26.38.22|겔 38:22⟧). It is used to express the idea of excruciating torment in ⟦66.14.10|계 14:10⟧; ⟦66.19.20|19:20⟧; ⟦66.20.10|20:10⟧.

A torrent.
1. Applied to small streams, as the Arnon, Jabbok, etc. Isaiah (15:7) speaks of the “book of the willows,” probably the Wady-el-Asha.
2. It is also applied to winter torrents (⟦18.6.15|욥 6:15⟧; ⟦4.34.5|민 34:5⟧; ⟦6.15.4|수 15:4⟧, ⟦6.15.47|47⟧), and to the torrent-bed or wady as well as to the torrent itself (⟦4.13.23|민 13:23⟧; ⟦11.17.3|왕상 17:3⟧).
3. In ⟦23.19.7|사 19:7⟧ the river Nile is meant, as rendered in the Revised Version.

1. In the natural and common sense (⟦40.1.2|마 1:2⟧; ⟦42.3.1|눅 3:1⟧, ⟦42.3.19|19⟧).
2. A near relation, a cousin (⟦1.13.8|창 13:8⟧; ⟦1.14.16|14:16⟧; ⟦40.12.46|마 12:46⟧; ⟦43.7.3|요 7:3⟧; ⟦44.1.14|행 1:14⟧; ⟦48.1.19|갈 1:19⟧).
3. Simply a fellow-countryman (⟦40.5.47|마 5:47⟧; ⟦44.3.22|행 3:22⟧; ⟦58.7.5|히 7:5⟧).
4. A disciple or follower (⟦40.25.40|마 25:40⟧; ⟦58.2.11|히 2:11⟧, ⟦58.2.12|12⟧).
5. One of the same faith (⟦30.1.9|암 1:9⟧; ⟦44.9.30|행 9:30⟧; ⟦44.11.29|11:29⟧; ⟦46.5.11|고전 5:11⟧); whence the early disciples of our Lord were known to each other as brethren.
6. A colleague in office (⟦15.3.2|스 3:2⟧; ⟦46.1.1|고전 1:1⟧; ⟦47.1.1|고후 1:1⟧).
7. A fellow-man (⟦1.9.5|창 9:5⟧; ⟦1.19.7|19:7⟧; ⟦40.5.22|마 5:22⟧, ⟦40.5.23|23⟧, ⟦40.5.24|24⟧; 7:5; ⟦58.2.17|히 2:17⟧).
8. One beloved or closely united with another in affection (⟦10.1.26|삼하 1:26⟧; ⟦44.6.3|행 6:3⟧; ⟦52.5.1|살전 5:1⟧). Brethren of Jesus (⟦40.1.25|마 1:25⟧; ⟦40.12.46|12:46⟧, ⟦40.12.50|50⟧: ⟦41.3.31|막 3:31⟧, ⟦41.3.32|32⟧; ⟦48.1.19|갈 1:19⟧; ⟦46.9.5|고전 9:5⟧, etc.) were probably the younger children of Joseph and Mary. Some have supposed that they may have been the children of Joseph by a former marriage, and others that they were the children of Mary, the Virgin’s sister, and wife of Cleophas. The first interpretation, however, is the most natural.
A vessel to draw water with (⟦23.40.15|사 40:15⟧); used figuratively, probably, of a numerous issue (⟦4.24.7|민 24:7⟧).

1. A portable shield (⟦10.22.31|삼하 22:31⟧; ⟦13.5.18|대상 5:18⟧).
2. A shield surrounding the person; the targe or round form; used once figuratively (⟦19.91.4|시 91:4⟧).
3. A large shield protecting the whole body (⟦19.35.2|시 35:2⟧; ⟦26.23.24|겔 23:24⟧; ⟦26.26.8|26:8⟧).
4. A lance or spear; improperly rendered “buckler” in the Authorized Version (⟦13.12.8|대상 12:8⟧), but correctly in the Revised Version “spear.”
 The leather of shields required oiling (⟦10.1.21|삼하 1:21⟧; ⟦23.21.5|사 21:5⟧), so as to prevent its being injured by moisture. Copper (= “brass”) shields were also in use (⟦9.17.6|삼상 17:6⟧; ⟦11.14.27|왕상 14:27⟧). Those spoken of in ⟦11.10.16|왕상 10:16⟧, etc.; 14:26, were probably of massive metal.
 The shields David had taken from his enemies were suspended in the temple as mementoes (⟦12.11.10|왕하 11:10⟧).

Among the Jews was suited to the climate and conditions of the country. They probably adopted the kind of architecture for their dwellings which they found already existing when they entered Canaan (⟦5.6.10|신 6:10⟧; ⟦4.13.19|민 13:19⟧). Phoenician artists (⟦10.5.11|삼하 5:11⟧; ⟦11.5.6|왕상 5:6⟧, ⟦11.5.18|18⟧) assisted at the erection of the royal palace and the temple at Jerusalem. Foreigners also assisted at the restoration of the temple after the Exile (⟦15.3.7|스 3:7⟧).
 In ⟦1.11.3|창 11:3⟧, ⟦1.11.9|9⟧, we have the first recorded instance of the erection of buildings. The cities of the plain of Shinar were founded by the descendants of Shem (10:11, 12, 22).
 The Israelites were by occupation shepherds and dwellers in tents (⟦1.47.3|창 47:3⟧); but from the time of their entering Canaan they became dwellers in towns, and in houses built of the native limestone of Palestine. Much building was carried on in Solomon’s time. Besides the buildings he completed at Jerusalem, he also built Baalath and Tadmor (⟦11.9.15|왕상 9:15⟧, ⟦11.9.24|24⟧). Many of the kings of Israel and Judah were engaged in erecting various buildings.
 Herod and his sons and successors restored the temple, and built fortifications and other structures of great magnificence in Jerusalem (⟦42.21.5|눅 21:5⟧).
 The instruments used in building are mentioned as the plumb-line (⟦30.7.7|암 7:7⟧), the measuring-reed (⟦26.40.3|겔 40:3⟧), and the saw (⟦11.7.9|왕상 7:9⟧).
 Believers are “God’s building” (⟦46.3.9|고전 3:9⟧); and heaven is called “a building of God” (⟦47.5.1|고후 5:1⟧). Christ is the only foundation of his church (⟦46.3.10|고전 3:10⟧), of which he also is the builder (⟦40.16.18|마 16:18⟧).
Rainy, the eighth ecclesiastical month of the year (⟦11.6.38|왕상 6:38⟧), and the second month of the civil year; later called Marchesvan (q.v.).

1. The translation of a word which is a generic name for horned cattle (⟦23.65.25|사 65:25⟧). It is also rendered “cow” (⟦26.4.15|겔 4:15⟧), “ox” (⟦1.12.16|창 12:16⟧).
2. The translation of a word always meaning an animal of the ox kind, without distinction of age or sex (⟦28.12.11|호 12:11⟧). It is rendered “cow” (⟦4.18.17|민 18:17⟧) and “ox” (⟦3.17.3|레 17:3⟧).
3. Another word is rendered in the same way (⟦24.31.18|렘 31:18⟧). It is also translated “calf” (⟦3.9.3|레 9:3⟧; ⟦33.6.6|미 6:6⟧). It is the same word used of the “molten calf” (⟦2.32.4|출 32:4⟧, ⟦2.32.8|8⟧) and “the golden calf” (⟦11.12.28|왕상 12:28⟧).
4. In ⟦7.6.25|삿 6:25⟧; ⟦23.34.7|사 34:7⟧, the Hebrew word is different. It is the customary word for bulls offered in sacrifice. In ⟦28.14.2|호 14:2⟧, the Authorized Version has “calves,” the Revised Version “bullocks.”

1. In ⟦23.58.5|사 58:5⟧ the rendering of a word which denotes “belonging to a marsh,” from the nature of the soil in which it grows (⟦23.18.2|사 18:2⟧). It was sometimes platted into ropes (⟦18.41.2|욥 41:2⟧; A.V., “hook,” R.V., “rope,” lit. “cord of rushes”).
2. In ⟦2.2.3|출 2:3⟧, ⟦23.18.2|사 18:2⟧ (R.V., “papyrus”) this word is the translation of the Hebrew gome, which designates the plant as absorbing moisture. In ⟦23.35.7|사 35:7⟧ and ⟦18.8.11|욥 8:11⟧ it is rendered “rush.” This was the Egyptian papyrus (papyrus Nilotica). It was anciently very abundant in Egypt. The Egyptians made garments and shoes and various utensils of it. It was used for the construction of the ark of Moses (⟦2.2.3|출 2:3⟧, ⟦2.2.5|5⟧). The root portions of the stem were used for food. The inside bark was cut into strips, which were sewed together and dried in the sun, forming the papyrus used for writing. It is no longer found in Egypt, but grows luxuriantly in Palestine, in the marshes of the Huleh, and in the swamps at the north end of the Lake of Gennesaret.

Mural towers, bastions, were introduced by king Uzziah (⟦14.26.15|대하 26:15⟧; ⟦36.1.16|습 1:16⟧; ⟦19.48.13|시 48:13⟧; ⟦23.26.1|사 26:1⟧). There are five Hebrew words so rendered in the Authorized Version, but the same word is also variously rendered.

1. A bundle of twigs (⟦2.12.22|출 12:22⟧).
2. Bunch or cake of raisins (⟦10.16.1|삼하 16:1⟧).
3. The “bunch of a camel” (⟦23.30.6|사 30:6⟧).

1. A load of any kind (⟦2.23.5|출 23:5⟧).
2. A severe task (⟦2.2.11|출 2:11⟧).
3. A difficult duty, requiring effort (⟦2.18.22|출 18:22⟧).
4. A prophecy of a calamitous or disastrous nature (⟦23.13.1|사 13:1⟧; ⟦23.17.1|17:1⟧; ⟦35.1.1|합 1:1⟧, etc.).

The first burial we have an account of is that of Sarah (⟦1.23.1|창 23장⟧). The first commercial transaction recorded is that of the purchase of a burial-place, for which Abraham weighed to Ephron “four hundred shekels of silver current money with the merchants.” Thus the patriarch became the owner of a part of the land of Canaan, the only part he ever possessed. When he himself died, “his sons Isaac and Ishmael buried him in the cave of Machpelah,” beside Sarah his wife (⟦1.25.9|창 25:9⟧).
 Deborah, Rebekah’s nurse, was buried under Allon-bachuth, “the oak of weeping” (⟦1.35.8|창 35:8⟧), near to Bethel. Rachel died, and was buried near Ephrath; “and Jacob set a pillar upon her grave” (16-20). Isaac was buried at Hebron, where he had died (27, 29). Jacob, when charging his sons to bury him in the cave of Machpelah, said, “There they buried Abraham and Sarah his wife; there they buried Isaac and Rebekah his wife; and there I buried Leah” (49:31). In compliance with the oath which he made him swear unto him (47:29-31), Joseph, assisted by his brethren, buried Jacob in the cave of Machpelah (50:2, 13). At the Exodus, Moses “took the bones of Joseph with him,” and they were buried in the “parcel of ground” which Jacob had bought of the sons of Hamor (⟦6.24.32|수 24:32⟧), which became Joseph’s inheritance (⟦1.48.22|창 48:22⟧; ⟦13.5.1|대상 5:1⟧; ⟦43.4.5|요 4:5⟧). Two burials are mentioned as having taken place in the wilderness. That of Miriam (⟦4.20.1|민 20:1⟧), and that of Moses, “in the land of Moab” (⟦5.34.5|신 34:5⟧, ⟦5.34.6|6⟧, ⟦5.34.8|8⟧). There is no account of the actual burial of Aaron, which probably, however, took place on the summit of Mount Hor (⟦4.20.28|민 20:28⟧, ⟦4.20.29|29⟧).
 Joshua was buried “in the border of his inheritance in Timnath-serah” (⟦6.24.1|수 24장⟧: 30).
 In Job we find a reference to burying-places, which were probably the Pyramids (3:14, 15). The Hebrew word for “waste places” here resembles in sound the Egyptian word for “pyramids.”
 Samuel, like Moses, was honoured with a national burial (⟦9.25.1|삼상 25:1⟧). Joab (⟦11.2.34|왕상 2:34⟧) “was buried in his own house in the wilderness.”
 In connection with the burial of Saul and his three sons we meet for the first time with the practice of burning the dead (⟦9.31.11|삼상 31:11⟧). The same practice is again referred to by Amos (6:10).
 Absalom was buried “in the wood” where he was slain (⟦10.18.17|삼하 18:17⟧, ⟦10.18.18|18⟧). The raising of the heap of stones over his grave was intended to mark abhorrence of the person buried (comp. ⟦6.7.26|수 7:26⟧ and 8:29). There was no fixed royal burying-place for the Hebrew kings. We find several royal burials taking place, however, “in the city of David” (⟦11.2.10|왕상 2:10⟧; ⟦11.11.43|11:43⟧; ⟦11.15.8|15:8⟧; ⟦12.14.19|왕하 14:19⟧, ⟦12.14.20|20⟧; ⟦12.15.38|15:38⟧; ⟦11.14.31|왕상 14:31⟧; ⟦11.22.50|22:50⟧; ⟦14.21.19|대하 21:19⟧, ⟦14.21.20|20⟧; ⟦14.24.25|대하 24:25⟧, etc.). Hezekiah was buried in the mount of the sepulchres of the sons of David; “and all Judah and the inhabitants of Jerusalem did him honour at his death” (⟦14.32.33|대하 32:33⟧).
 Little is said regarding the burial of the kings of Israel. Some of them were buried in Samaria, the capital of their kingdom (⟦12.10.35|왕하 10:35⟧; ⟦12.13.9|13:9⟧; ⟦12.14.16|14:16⟧).
 Our Lord was buried in a new tomb, hewn out of the rock, which Joseph of Arimathea had prepared for himself (⟦40.27.57|마 27:57⟧; ⟦41.15.46|막 15:46⟧; ⟦43.19.41|요 19:41⟧, ⟦43.19.42|42⟧).
 The grave of Lazarus was “a cave, and a stone lay on it” (⟦43.11.38|요 11:38⟧). Graves were frequently either natural caverns or artificial excavations formed in the sides of rocks (⟦1.23.9|창 23:9⟧; ⟦40.27.60|마 27:60⟧); and coffins were seldom used, unless when the body was brought from a distance.

Hebrew olah; i.e., “ascending,” the whole being consumed by fire, and regarded as ascending to God while being consumed. Part of every offering was burnt in the sacred fire, but this was wholly burnt, a “whole burnt offering.” It was the most frequent form of sacrifice, and apparently the only one mentioned in the book of Genesis. Such were the sacrifices offered by Abel (⟦1.4.3|창 4:3⟧, ⟦1.4.4|4⟧, here called minhah; i.e., “a gift”), Noah (⟦1.8.20|창 8:20⟧), Abraham (⟦1.22.2|창 22:2⟧, ⟦1.22.7|7⟧, ⟦1.22.8|8⟧, ⟦1.22.13|13⟧), and by the Hebrews in Egypt (⟦2.10.25|출 10:25⟧).
 The law of Moses afterwards prescribed the occasions and the manner in which burnt sacrifices were to be offered. There were “the continual burnt offering” (⟦2.29.38|출 29:38⟧; ⟦3.6.9|레 6:9⟧), “the burnt offering of every sabbath,” which was double the daily one (⟦4.28.9|민 28:9⟧, ⟦4.28.10|10⟧), “the burnt offering of every month” (28:11-15), the offerings at the Passover (19-23), at Pentecost (⟦3.23.16|레 23:16⟧), the feast of Trumpets (23:23-25), and on the day of Atonement (⟦3.16.1|레 16장⟧).
 On other occasions special sacrifices were offered, as at the consecration of Aaron (⟦2.29.1|출 29장⟧) and the dedication of the temple (⟦11.8.5|왕상 8:5⟧, ⟦11.8.62|62⟧-64).
 Free-will burnt offerings were also permitted (⟦3.1.13|레 1:13⟧), and were offered at the accession of Solomon to the throne (⟦13.29.21|대상 29:21⟧), and at the reformation brought about by Hezekiah (⟦14.29.1|대하 29장⟧: 31-35).
 These offerings signified the complete dedication of the offerers unto God. This is referred to in ⟦45.12.1|롬 12:1⟧. (See ALTAR, SACRIFICE.)

In which Jehovah appeared to Moses in the wilderness (⟦2.3.2|출 3:2⟧; ⟦44.7.30|행 7:30⟧). It is difficult to say what particular kind of plant or bush is here meant. Probably it was the mimosa or acacia. The words “in the bush” in ⟦41.12.26|막 12:26⟧; ⟦42.20.37|눅 20:37⟧, mean “in the passage or paragraph on the bush;” i.e., in ⟦2.3.1|출 3장⟧.

Properly a servant in charge of the wine (⟦1.40.1|창 40:1⟧; ⟦1.41.9|41:9⟧). The Hebrew word, mashkeh, thus translated is rendered also (plural) “cup-bearers” (⟦11.10.5|왕상 10:5⟧; ⟦14.9.4|대하 9:4⟧). Nehemiah (1:11) was cup-bearer to king Artaxerxes. It was a position of great responsibility and honour in royal households.

(Heb. hemah), curdled milk (⟦1.18.8|창 18:8⟧; ⟦7.5.25|삿 5:25⟧; ⟦10.17.29|삼하 17:29⟧), or butter in the form of the skim of hot milk or cream, called by the Arabs kaimak, a semi-fluid (⟦18.20.17|욥 20:17⟧; ⟦18.29.6|29:6⟧; ⟦5.32.14|신 32:14⟧). The words of ⟦20.30.33|잠 30:33⟧ have been rendered by some “the pressure [not churning] of milk bringeth forth cheese.”

Hebrew millah (⟦18.30.9|욥 30:9⟧), a word or speech, and hence object of talk; Hebrew mashal (⟦19.44.14|시 44:14⟧), a proverb or parable. When it denotes a sharp word of derision, as in ⟦5.28.37|신 28:37⟧, ⟦5.28.1|1⟧ Kings 9:7, ⟦14.7.20|대하 7:20⟧, the Hebrew sheninah is used. In ⟦24.24.9|렘 24:9⟧ it is rendered “taunt.”
Hollow (R.V., “kab”), occurs only in ⟦12.6.25|왕하 6:25⟧; a dry measure, the sixth part of a seah, and the eighteenth part of an ephah, equal to about two English quarts.

How little! as nothing.
1. A town on the eastern border of Asher (⟦6.19.27|수 19:27⟧), probably one of the towns given by Solomon to Hiram; the modern Kabul, some 8 miles east of Accho, on the very borders of Galilee.
2. A district in the north-west of Galilee, near to Tyre, containing twenty cities given to Hiram by Solomon as a reward for various services rendered to him in building the temple (⟦11.9.13|왕상 9:13⟧), and as payment of the six score talents of gold he had borrowed from him. Hiram gave the cities this name because he was not pleased with the gift, the name signifying “good for nothing.” Hiram seems afterwards to have restored these cities to Solomon (⟦14.8.2|대하 8:2⟧).

The title assumed by the Roman emperors after Julius Caesar. In the New Testament this title is given to various emperors as sovereigns of Judaea without their accompanying distinctive proper names (⟦43.19.15|요 19:15⟧; ⟦44.17.7|행 17:7⟧). The Jews paid tribute to Caesar (⟦40.22.17|마 22:17⟧), and all Roman citizens had the right of appeal to him (⟦44.25.11|행 25:11⟧). The Caesars referred to in the New Testament are Augustus (⟦42.2.1|눅 2:1⟧), Tiberius (3:1; 20:22), Claudius (⟦44.11.28|행 11:28⟧), and Nero (⟦44.25.8|행 25:8⟧; ⟦50.4.22|빌 4:22⟧).

A city on the northeast of the marshy plain of el-Huleh, 120 miles north of Jerusalem, and 20 miles north of the Sea of Galilee, at the “upper source” of the Jordan, and near the base of Mount Hermon. It is mentioned in ⟦40.16.13|마 16:13⟧ and ⟦41.8.27|막 8:27⟧ as the northern limit of our Lord’s public ministry. According to some its original name was Baal-Gad (⟦6.11.17|수 11:17⟧), or Baal-Hermon (⟦7.3.3|삿 3:3⟧; ⟦13.5.23|대상 5:23⟧), when it was a Canaanite sanctuary of Baal. It was afterwards called Panium or Paneas, from a deep cavern full of water near the town. This name was given to the cavern by the Greeks of the Macedonian kingdom of Antioch because of its likeness to the grottos of Greece, which were always associated with the worship of their god Pan. Its modern name is Banias. Here Herod built a temple, which he dedicated to Augustus Caesar. This town was afterwards enlarged and embellished by Herod Philip, the tetrarch of Trachonitis, of whose territory it formed a part, and was called by him Caesarea Philippi, partly after his own name, and partly after that of the emperor Tiberius Caesar. It is thus distinguished from the Caesarea of Palestine.

(Palestinae), a city on the shore of the Mediterranean, on the great road from Tyre to Egypt, about 70 miles northwest of Jerusalem, at the northern extremity of the plain of Sharon. It was built by Herod the Great (B.C. 10), who named it after Caesar Augustus, hence called Caesarea Sebaste (Gr. Sebastos = “Augustus”), on the site of an old town called “Strato’s Tower.” It was the capital of the Roman province of Judaea, the seat of the governors or procurators, and the headquarters of the Roman troops. It was the great Gentile city of Palestine, with a spacious artificial harbour. It was adorned with many buildings of great splendour, after the manner of the Roman cities of the West. Here Cornelius the centurion was converted through the instrumentality of Peter (⟦44.10.1|행 10:1⟧, ⟦44.10.24|24⟧), and thus for the first time the door of faith was opened to the Gentiles. Philip the evangelist resided here with his four daughters (21:8). From this place Saul sailed for his native Tarsus when forced to flee from Jerusalem (9:30), and here he landed when returning from his second missionary journey (18:22). He remained as a prisoner here for two years before his voyage to Rome (⟦44.24.27|행 24:27⟧; ⟦44.25.1|25:1⟧, ⟦44.25.4|4⟧, ⟦44.25.6|6⟧, ⟦44.25.13|13⟧). Here on a “set day,” when games were celebrated in the theatre in honour of the emperor Claudius, Herod Agrippa I. appeared among the people in great pomp, and in the midst of the idolatrous homage paid to him was suddenly smitten by an angel, and carried out a dying man. He was “eaten of worms” (12:19-23), thus perishing by the same loathsome disease as his granfather, Herod the Great. It still retains its ancient name Kaiseriyeh, but is now desolate. “The present inhabitants of the ruins are snakes, scorpions, lizards, wild boars, and jackals.” It is described as the most desolate city of all Palestine.

(Heb. kelub’, ⟦24.5.27|렘 5:27⟧, marg. “coop;” rendered “basket” in ⟦30.8.1|암 8:1⟧), a basket of wicker-work in which birds were placed after being caught. In ⟦66.18.2|계 18:2⟧ it is the rendering of the Greek phulake, properly a prison or place of confinement.
